Nawah runs a real Linux distribution on your phone — Debian or Ubuntu, with a full XFCE desktop — inside a single app. No root, and no second app to install.\n\nIt works by running the distribution under proot, a userspace sandbox that needs no kernel privileges, and drawing its desktop through an X server built into this app.

proot traces every system call, so a heavy build is noticeably slower than on a laptop. There is no GPU acceleration: the desktop is drawn in software. Memory cannot be capped — that needs cgroups, and cgroups need root. The camera is not reachable from inside the container.\n\nNone of this is a bug list. It is what running Linux without root costs, and the app is built to be honest about it rather than to hide it.

Abdullah — a student, and a technical researcher who likes understanding systems from the inside rather than using them from the outside.\n\nNawah started from one question: can a phone be a real computer, without asking anyone\'s permission?
This app would not exist without three projects, and it ships their code:
proot — the userspace sandbox that runs the distribution. GPL-2.0.
termux-x11 (lorie) — the X server that draws the desktop. GPL-3.0.
busybox — the small tools the container starts with. GPL-2.0.

Nawah is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later. You may use, study, share and modify it — and if you distribute a modified version, you must share its source under the same licence.\n\nThis is not a choice of style: proot and busybox are GPL-2.0 and the X server is GPL-3.0, so anything that ships them must be too.
Everything is drawn in software here — the lighter the desktop, the better it feels.
Serial adapters, Arduino and ESP boards.
Nothing attached.\n\nPlug a board in with an OTG cable. Serial adapters — Arduino, ESP32, CH340, FTDI, CP210x — appear here.

Android will not let a program inside the system open a USB device — only the app can, and only after you allow it. So the app holds the device and presents it inside Linux as %1$s, a real serial port. screen, minicom, pyserial, arduino-cli and stty work unchanged, and the speed you set inside Linux is applied to the device.

A Linux pseudo-terminal carries no DTR or RTS line — the kernel simply does not implement it for these devices. So avrdude and esptool cannot reset a board through the port. Reset it from inside Linux first:

 nawah-usb reset an Arduino
 nawah-usb reset-esp an ESP32

then run the tool with its own no-reset option.
